newsitem.title: SPAIN: Pro-ETA protests barred for fear of violence.
newsitem.headline: Pro-ETA protests barred for fear of violence.

text.p: The Basque government on Wednesday barred the political wing of the guerrilla group ETA from going ahead with demonstrations this weekend, fearing a new wave of violence following the rebels' killing of a young politician.

With Spain still seething with anger over the murder of Miguel Angel Blanco, officials in the Basque region said they would not allow pro-ETA rallies planned for San Sebastian, a stronghold of the radical separatist movement.
"Given the social tension over the murder of the councillor, it is likely there will be incidents during the demonstration," the Basque Interior Ministry said in an official decree.
Millions of Spaniards have vented their outrage against ETA in mostly peaceful demonstrations since the death of the 29-year-old politician, who was kidnapped last Thursday and shot 48 hours later.
But there have also been sporadic attacks against ETA sympathisers and the offices of the rebels' political arm, Herri Batasuna.

Authorities feared that pro-ETA demonstrations so soon after Blanco's death could unleash a wave of sectarian clashes that could spread from the Basque country of northern Spain throughout the country.
Herri Batasuna has urged its supporters to demonstrate on Saturday and Sunday for "liberty and democracy." Despite the government ban, there was no immediate word on whether it would call it off.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and other Spanish leaders have branded them "accomplices" to Blanco's murder. But Herri Batasuna claims it is being targeted for a "political lynching."
The radical political party won nearly 15 percent of the Basque vote in the 1995 election. It holds in the national congress and in the Basque and Navarre regional parliaments.

Spanish Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja praised the Basque government's decision, telling reporters: "This is a prudent act and it shows that the thousands and thousands who demonstrated in the streets (against ETA) did not do so in vain."

Mayor Oreja said the government was preparing legal reforms aimed at ETA sympathisers that would strengthen laws against those who encourage or "defend" acts of terrorism. One measure would tighten restrictions on pro-ETA demonstrations.
Adding his voice to the outcry against ETA, Spain's King Juan Carlos declared on Wednesday that Blanco's murder was "as contemptible as the terrorists who killed him."
The speech, delivered in Berlin and broadcast on Spanish national radio, was the strongest condemnation of ETA yet by the king, who normally tries to stay out of politics.

Spaniards have in the past endured vicious attacks by ETA, which has killed nearly 800 people in its 29-year struggle for independence. But it was the death sentence carried out against an ordinary, low-ranking functionary that cut to the heart of Spanish society.

Blanco, a Basque town councillor and a member of Spain's ruling party, was abducted by ETA rebels who vowed to kill him if the government did not move 500 rebel inmates to prisons in the Basque region within 48 hours. They shot him twice in the head on Saturday, and he died 12 hours later.
More than two million people took to the streets across Spain on Monday after Blanco's funeral, and hundreds of thousands more demonstrated on Tuesday in several cities.

"I will only say that if the death of my son has served to unite the Basque country, Spain and the whole world and it ends all the bad in the world, my son's death is welcome," Blanco's mother said in a radio interview.

But the public outcry did not deter the guerrillas from issuing a death threat against a second Basque politician, 63-year-old Jose Luis Caso. The Basque town councillor, a member of the ruling party in Renteria, has been given bodyguards.

France's Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou pledged on Monday to expedite the extradition of ETA members wanted in Spain. The rebels have traditionally used southwest France as a base for attacks across the border.
